About Me

Chenglong Yan

严成龙

Master’s student · Guangzhou University

I am a master’s student in Cartography and Geographic Information Systems at Guangzhou University, affiliated with the School of Geography and Remote Sensing and the Institute of Aerospace Remote Sensing Innovations. I am advised by Prof. Xingfa Gu and Dr. Dakang Wang. Previously, I received my B.S. in Geographic Information Science from Beibu Gulf University.

My research focuses on atmospheric remote sensing, air pollution monitoring, and atmospheric chemistry modeling. I combine OMI and TROPOMI observations, GEOS-Chem simulations, and machine learning to study the spatiotemporal evolution of atmospheric trace gases.

Published Article

Journal of Environmental Management2026416: 130786

Projected westward advance of tropospheric formaldehyde over China

Chenglong Yan, Hui Xia, Gonzalo González Abad, Dakang Wang, Michel Van Roozendael, Yibo Wang, Xicheng Li, Wenfu Sun, Xiaoxing Zuo, Xiankun Yang, Jinnian Wang, Xingfa Gu

OMI observations and a surface-to-line machine learning approach reveal the evolving westward boundary of tropospheric formaldehyde across China.

Paper
Abstract

Economic development and population aggregation are driving the east-to-west spread of tropospheric formaldehyde (HCHO) in China; yet the historical trajectory and future threat of this westward migration remain poorly understood. Here, we analyze OMI satellite observations utilizing a novel surface-to-line differentiation approach and machine learning to project spatiotemporal distribution of tropospheric formaldehyde in China, measure the westward movement of formaldehyde using the classic Hu Huanyong Line (Hu Line). We show that high-HCHO boundary migrated from 132.7 km east of the Hu Line in 2005 to 130.2 km west of it in 2020, before a subsequent partial eastward retreat to 6.6–87.8 km. The westward migration rate peaked at 25.12 km yr⁻¹ during 2010–2014, then progressively slowed and became negative after 2020, reaching −8.48 km yr⁻¹. This trajectory reflects a fundamental transition from strong coupling to decoupling between economic expansion and pollution spread. Regionally, the strongest westward advance occurred over the Heilongjiang–Jilin and Shanxi–Shaanxi energy base, whereas the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region exhibited early contraction. Our research quantifies the risks of transregional HCHO transport and provides a scientific foundation for predictive air quality management and regional governance, and these findings also demonstrate that the Hu Line should be an environmentally dynamic boundary reflecting regional economic activity, providing a new perspective for assessing sustainable development patterns and human–environment interactions.
